routes.label: Compare common arcs and unfold the zigzags

question:
Sergei skated around an ice rink, gliding along different paths. The marked lines in the figures below show four of the paths labeled P, Q, R, and S. What is the sorted order of the four paths from shortest to longest?

[Figure 1](figures/2024_AMC_8_Q06_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Paths \(P\), \(Q\), and \(S\) follow the same two rounded ends, so we can compare their straight portions first. Let \(h>0\) be the length of a straight side of the rink, and let \(w>0\) be the width between the straight sides.

Path \(P\) has two straight portions of length \(h\), totaling \(2h\). Path \(S\) has two diagonals across the central rectangle. By the Pythagorean theorem, their total length is
\[
2\sqrt{h^2+w^2}>2h.
\]
Adding the common end arcs shows that \(P<S\).

The four diagonal pieces of \(Q\) form two zigzags. Each zigzag goes from a top corner to the bottom corner on the same side, visiting the opposite side once. To compare one zigzag with a diagonal, reflect its portion after that visit across the opposite vertical side. Reflection preserves length and leaves the turning point fixed. The reflected bottom endpoint is now \(2w\) horizontally from the starting point and \(h\) below it.

The reflected broken path is at least as long as the straight segment between its endpoints. Thus each zigzag has length at least \(\sqrt{h^2+4w^2}\), and the straight portions of \(Q\) total at least
\[
2\sqrt{h^2+4w^2}
>2\sqrt{h^2+w^2}.
\]
This proves \(S<Q\). The argument does not require either turning point to be at the midpoint of a side.

Finally, \(R\) uses the same vertical portions as \(P\). At each rounded end, it replaces the curved route with two straight chords. Each chord is shorter than its corresponding arc because a straight segment is the shortest path between its endpoints. Therefore \(R<P\).

Combining the comparisons gives \(\boxed{R<P<S<Q}\), so the order is \(R,P,S,Q\), choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
